titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Sunday, 7 August 1921
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I wonder if you are back in London and have received the Italian papers I sent for the second time. I should like to have them back later on by post or in a letter. Parcels seem to take six weeks to travel.

seg.quote: I have had five weeks of delightful vacation with my eyes … The subscriptions have been rather slow and poor and now seem to have come or be coming to an end.

div.p: I believe some 5000 prospectuses were sent out and the capture is 260 but people ought not to be told this figure.

seg.quote: I am trying to make up for lost time. … About three months ago I received a note of four lines from Mr Pinker to which I replied by a note of no lines at all – which is shorter still. I think it would be well if Ulysses makes my name to unify my publishers.

div.p: Mr Mathews and Mr Richards are two bores quite as incompetent as my agent and swindlers into the bargain. Perhaps they could be induced to pass over their rights and remainders of copies to you. The former never paid me any royalties on either edition, from the latter I got about £10 in as many years. Mr Huebsch began rather well but has changed his mind. Whether he sends any royalties to Mr Pinker or not I don’t know. Perhaps he does. I daresay my agent will hold them up until I reply to his fourlined note of challenge.

seg.quote: I was going to take a forty-eight hour holiday somewhere but decided not to do so. … Bloom and all the Blooms will soon be dead, thank God. Everyone says he ought to have died long ago.

div.p: I shall return to the subject of our last letters shortly but not today. I heard still another description of myself as a very elegant fashionable person. I hope you will laugh as much at this as I did.

div.note: In early July, JJ suffered an attack of iritis, from which he spent five weeks recovering with the aid of repeated doses of cocaine to relieve the pain (JJ 517).

When plans for an American publication fell through, Sylvia Beach offered JJ to publish Ulysses in Paris. The plan was for a first edition of 1,000 copies, to be sold in advance by subscription. A four-page prospectus was mailed to several hundred people and shops in England and in France that had expressed interest and might subscribe to Ulysses. The names of the persons and shops in England were supplied to Beach by Harriet Weaver (JJ 506). An image of the prospectus can be found on the website of the British Library.

Harriet Weaver had expressed alarm after hearing rumours about JJ’s excessive drinking habits (JJ 509). JJ replied with a lengthy letter enumerating preposterous “legends” that supposedly had been circulating about him in various countries and bemoaned the lack of support in Paris for his work (JJ to Harriet Weaver, 24 June 1921 [SL 281-84]).
